title: Merge Intervals
directAnswer: Sort the intervals by start, then sweep left-to-right keeping one 'current' merged interval. If the next interval starts at or before the current interval's end, extend the current end to the max of the two ends; otherwise the current interval is final — push it and start a new one. O(n log n) for the sort, O(n) for the sweep.

remember.pattern: Sort by start, then linear sweep-merge
rules: **Sort by start first** — without it the sweep is meaningless because a later overlapper could appear anywhere.
Overlap test after sorting collapses to one comparison: `iv.start <= last.end`. You never need to check the start side.
When merging, take `max(last.end, iv.end)` — the next interval can be fully *inside* the current one (don't shrink the end).
Compare against the **last merged** interval, not the previous raw interval — merging can keep extending the same bucket.
Use `<=` (not `<`) so touching intervals like `[1,4]` and `[4,5]` fuse into `[1,5]`.
whenToUse: A pile of unsorted intervals you must collapse into disjoint ones
Calendar consolidation, free/busy merging, range coalescing
Output must itself be sorted and non-overlapping
antiSignals: Input is already sorted + one insert → Insert Interval's O(n) sweep (LC 57)
You only need the count of rooms / max overlap → sweep-line or heap, not a merge
You must remove the fewest intervals to make them disjoint → greedy by end (LC 435)
Endpoints are exclusive → switch the overlap test to strict `<`
remember.takeaway: Sorting by start is what turns interval problems from O(n²) pair-checking into an O(n) sweep — after sorting, the only interval that can overlap the current one is the next one. Merge Intervals is THE template; Insert Interval, Non-overlapping Intervals, and Meeting Rooms are all variations on this sweep.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reach for 'sort by start, then sweep' on overlapping ranges — and whether you correctly take max(end) when merging instead of blindly using the later interval's end.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Comparing each interval to the previous *raw* interval instead of the last *merged* one, or using the new interval's end directly so a fully-contained interval shrinks the merged range.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State why sorting by start makes the overlap check one-sided, handle the contained-interval case explicitly with max(end), and note the O(n log n) is sort-bound so it can't be beaten without sorted input.

problemStatement:
Given an array of `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [startᵢ, endᵢ]`, **merge all overlapping intervals**, and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input.

Two intervals overlap if they share any point, including a single shared endpoint — so `[1,4]` and `[4,5]` merge into `[1,5]`.
constraints: The returned list must be sorted and non-overlapping
understanding: You have a messy set of ranges that may overlap in any combination. Collapse every cluster of overlapping ranges into a single range that spans the cluster, and return the cleaned, disjoint, sorted set. The merged set covers exactly the same points as the original.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the input sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — that's the key difference from Insert Interval. We pay an O(n log n) sort up front, which is what makes the single sweep correct.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do intervals that only touch at an endpoint count as overlapping?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes for this problem — [1,4] and [4,5] merge into [1,5]. That means the overlap test uses `<=`, not strict `<`.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can one interval be completely inside another?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — [1,10] and [3,5]. When merging we take max of the ends so the bigger interval isn't shrunk by the contained one.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I mutate / sort the input array in place?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Usually fine, and it saves memory. Confirm, but sorting in place is the standard approach here.

examples.explanation: [1,3] and [2,6] overlap (2 ≤ 3) → [1,6]. The other two are disjoint.
They touch at 4. Because touching counts as overlapping, they merge into [1,5].
[2,3] is fully inside [1,4]. Taking max(4,3)=4 keeps the larger interval intact.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Repeatedly Fuse Any Overlapping Pair
approaches.whenToMention: Mention to show you understand what 'merge' means mechanically — then discard it as quadratic.
hints: Two intervals overlap iff a.start ≤ b.end AND b.start ≤ a.end. How would you fuse every overlapping pair with no sorting at all?
Repeatedly scan all pairs; whenever two overlap, replace them with their union and restart.
It's correct but you re-scan the whole set every time you fuse — that's where the quadratic blow-up comes from.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each fuse can trigger a fresh O(n) pass and there can be O(n) fuses, giving O(n²). The sorted approach removes the need to ever look backwards.
approaches.explanation:
Without sorting, an overlapping partner could sit anywhere in the list, so the naive idea is to keep scanning all pairs and fuse any two that overlap, repeating until a full pass makes no change.

**Why it works.** Overlap is symmetric and 'mergeability' is transitive across a cluster, so repeatedly unioning any overlapping pair eventually collapses each cluster to one interval. The two-sided overlap test `a.start <= b.end && b.start <= a.end` is the honest definition when nothing is sorted.

**Why we abandon it.** Every fuse can invalidate earlier comparisons, forcing another full O(n) sweep, and there can be O(n) fuses — so the whole thing is O(n²). The fix is not a smarter pairwise check; it's to *sort first* so that overlapping intervals become adjacent and a single forward pass suffices.
approaches.insight: The pain here is that overlaps can hide anywhere, so you keep looking backwards. Sorting by start eliminates 'backwards' entirely: after sorting, if an interval overlaps the current cluster at all, it overlaps the most recent merged interval — so one forward scan is enough.

dryRun.intro: Scan all pairs, fuse on overlap, repeat. Notice how unsorted order forces extra passes.

steps.action: a full pass made no fuse → stop

python.explanation: Symmetric overlap check; either interval may come first.

edgeCases.behavior: Pair overlaps; union = [min(1,2), max(4,3)] = [1,4]. Contained interval doesn't shrink the result.
No pair overlaps; the first full pass makes no fuse → returns input unchanged.

pitfalls: Using the later interval's end directly instead of max — shrinks the result on contained intervals.
Forgetting to restart after a fuse — a new union can overlap an interval you already passed.
Treating O(n²) as acceptable just because it passes small cases.

approaches.name: Sort by Start, then Sweep-Merge (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The canonical answer. Lead with 'sort by start, then I only ever compare to the last merged interval'.
hints: If the intervals were sorted by start, where is the only place an overlap with the current cluster can appear?
Sort by start. Keep a result list; for each interval, either it extends the last merged interval (start ≤ last end) or it begins a fresh one.
When it extends, set last.end = max(last.end, cur.end) — the current interval might be entirely inside the last.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting is O(n log n) and dominates; the sweep visits each interval once doing O(1) work, O(n). Output (and the sort) need O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Sort the intervals by start, then walk once keeping a result list whose last element is the 'current' open interval.

**Why sorting makes the check one-sided.** After sorting by start, every interval we visit has a start ≥ every interval already processed. So the *only* way the current interval can overlap the existing merged set is by overlapping the most recent merged interval. That collapses the honest two-sided overlap test down to a single comparison: `cur.start <= last.end`. No need to look backwards, no need to check the start side — sorting bought us that.

**The sweep.** For each interval `cur`: if the result is empty or `cur.start > last.end`, there's a gap, so `cur` is a brand-new disjoint interval — append it. Otherwise they overlap (or touch), so extend the current interval: `last.end = max(last.end, cur.end)`.

**Why `max(last.end, cur.end)` and not just `cur.end`.** A sorted-by-start interval can still be fully *contained* in the current one — e.g. current `[1,10]`, next `[3,5]`. Writing `last.end = cur.end` would shrink `[1,10]` to `[1,5]` and lose coverage. Taking the max keeps whichever end reaches further right. This single `max` is the line most candidates get wrong under pressure.
approaches.insight: The whole trick is that *sorting localizes overlap*. Before sorting, an overlapping partner can be anywhere, forcing O(n²) pair checks; after sorting, it can only be the neighbor you just merged. That 'sort to make the relevant thing adjacent' move is the beating heart of nearly every interval problem — internalize it once and Insert Interval, Non-overlapping Intervals, and both Meeting Rooms variants all fall out of it.

pitfalls: Forgetting to sort — the one-sided overlap check is only valid on sorted input.
Writing `last.end = cur.end` instead of `max(...)` — shrinks on contained intervals.
Using `<` instead of `<=` in the merge test — fails to fuse touching intervals like [1,4] and [4,5].

commonMistakes: Comparing to the previous raw interval instead of the last merged interval.
Using cur.end directly instead of max(last.end, cur.end), shrinking on contained intervals.
Forgetting to sort by start before sweeping.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Using the new interval's end instead of the max
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A sorted interval can be fully inside the current one ([1,10] then [3,5]). Assigning cur.end directly shrinks [1,10] to [1,5] and loses coverage.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if cur[0] <= res[-1][1]:
    res[-1][1] = cur[1]            # shrinks on [1,10] then [3,5]

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparing to the previous interval, not the last merged one
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Three intervals can chain-merge ([1,5],[2,8],[7,9]). Comparing each to its raw predecessor instead of the growing merged tail breaks the chain.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
int[] last = res.get(res.size() - 1);
if (cur[0] <= last[1]) { last[1] = Math.max(last[1], cur[1]); }

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Skipping the sort
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The single one-sided overlap test (cur.start <= last.end) is only correct once intervals are sorted by start. On unsorted input it misses overlaps that appear out of order.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
res = []
for cur in intervals:           # no sort
    ...
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
intervals.sort(key=lambda iv: iv[0])
res = []
for cur in intervals:
    ...
